comparison: Perfect agreement. Both evaluations support claims C40-C45 regarding the modified avoidance task with shortened/extended tones and the linear regression analysis showing PV activity is better explained by avoidance movement than tone offset. Peer reviewer 1 explicitly affirms 'good controls to rule out a role for cue offset.'

Disagreement on interpretation. Both address claims C4, C30-C31, C54-C59 regarding temporal dissociation between PV activity emergence and avoidance learning. OpenEval finds this strongly supports the freezing suppression interpretation. However, peer reviewer 1 identifies this as 'UNCERTAIN' noting 'discordance between changes in neural activity and behavior' - PV activity emerges immediately but avoidance learning is gradual. Reviewer acknowledges 'plausible explanations' but questions the interpretation.

Perfect agreement. Both evaluations support claims C76-C77 showing no effect when optogenetic stimulation occurs after avoidance. Both interpret this as supporting that PV activity is important during avoidance movement itself, not for subsequent learning.

Strong agreement. Both evaluations support claims C7, C33-C34, C60, C63, C66-C68 regarding optogenetic suppression delaying avoidance and increasing freezing. OpenEval also includes C69 (mechanistic interpretation). All peer reviewers affirm the causal manipulation findings as 'compelling' and 'consistent with the conceptual model.'

Strong agreement. Both evaluations support claims C70-C74 regarding block structure analysis showing immediate effects on first stimulation trial and immediate reversal. OpenEval also includes C75. Both interpret this as evidence for real-time behavioral role rather than learning effect.

Strong agreement. Both evaluations support claims C3, C27, C37 regarding fiber photometry data showing IL PV activity rises during avoidance movements. OpenEval also includes C38-C39 (lack of correlation with movement parameters). Peer reviewers describe methods as 'appropriate,' experiments as 'well done,' and evidence as 'compelling.'

Strong agreement. Both evaluations support claims C8, C61, C64 showing no effect of IL PV suppression on reward approach. OpenEval finds this demonstrates specificity to threat-related contexts. Peer reviewer 2 affirms 'extensive experiments demonstrate the mechanism is selective for avoidance under threat, not reward settings.'

Strong agreement. Both evaluations support claims C47-C50 regarding post-crossing signal that occurs with and without reward delivery. OpenEval addresses broader context (C5, C28, C46) about lack of elevated activity during reward approach. Both acknowledge C50 is appropriately speculative.

Strong agreement. Both evaluations support the main interpretive conclusions (C10, C35, C65, C69, C81) that IL PV neurons suppress freezing to enable avoidance. OpenEval includes additional claims (C32, C85, C87-C88). All peer reviewers affirm this as 'compelling evidence' and 'consistent with the conceptual model.' Editor describes it as an 'important study.'

Strong agreement. Both evaluations support claims C6, C29, C51 regarding no elevated IL PV activity during movement in open field. OpenEval also includes C52 (contextual interpretation). Peer reviewers affirm these as 'good controls to rule out nonspecific role in movement initiation.'

Disagreement on certainty. Both address mechanistic interpretation claims C36, C103-C104. OpenEval finds these 'SUPPORTED' as reasonable extensions of the data. Peer reviewers rate as 'UNCERTAIN,' noting 'potential mechanisms are discussed but not directly examined' and 'exact mechanisms are not explored.' OpenEval also includes C89, C101-C102.

Strong agreement. Both evaluations support claims C38-C39 showing PV activity is not correlated with movement parameters and does not change with learning. OpenEval groups these with C3, C27, C37. Peer reviewers affirm these findings support the freezing suppression interpretation.

Strong agreement. Both evaluations support claims C9, C62 showing no effect of IL PV suppression on locomotion in open field. OpenEval also includes C61, C64. Peer reviewers affirm this demonstrates specificity to threat circumstances.

Strong agreement. Both evaluations support claims C5, C28, C46 regarding no elevated IL PV activity during reward approach. OpenEval groups these with post-crossing signal claims (C47-C50). Peer reviewers affirm 'extensive experiments demonstrate selectivity for threat, not reward settings.'

Partial overlap. OpenEval supports claims C94-C100 as providing discussion context with appropriate citations, including C100 on synchronization hypothesis. Peer reviewers address C100 (along with C36, C103-C104) as 'UNCERTAIN' because mechanistic interpretations are not directly tested.

OpenEval supports claims C86, C90-C93 regarding arguments against the safety signal hypothesis, finding them well-supported by temporal dynamics and lack of learning-related changes. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval supports claims C1-C2, C11-C16 as background context with appropriate citations establishing study rationale. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval supports claims C17-C20, C82-C84 as established background on active avoidance behavior with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval supports claims C21-C23 as background on IL function with appropriate citations, noting C23 is appropriately presented as theoretical model. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval supports claims C24-C26 as background on PV neuron function, noting C26 is appropriately presented as theoretical model. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval supports claims C105-C112 as essential methodological details clearly stated in Materials and Methods. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval supports claim C53 as explicitly presented hypothesis that is reasonable and subsequently tested in Figure 4 experiments. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
